subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Cobalt Problem
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Cobalt Problem.

hook.text: Over 70 percent of the world's cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

buildup.text: Some cobalt is mined by hand in artisanal mines where safety regulations barely exist.

discovery.text: Reports of child labor in Congolese cobalt mines shocked consumers and pressured automakers to act.

twist.text: Companies are racing to reduce cobalt in batteries, but eliminating it entirely is chemically difficult.

climax.text: LFP batteries use zero cobalt, giving ethical buyers a clear alternative as the chemistry improves.

punchline.text: The darkest chapter of EV batteries is slowly being rewritten.

quiz.question: Where does the majority of the world's cobalt come from?

details.summary: Cobalt is a critical but controversial battery material. Much of it is mined in the Congo under harsh conditions, driving the industry to develop cobalt-free or low-cobalt battery chemistries.
details.whyItMatters: The ethical and supply-chain risks of cobalt dependence threaten the credibility of EVs as a clean technology. Reducing cobalt usage is both a moral imperative and a strategic business decision.
takeaways: Over 70 percent of cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo
Artisanal mining in the Congo involves serious human rights issues
LFP and high-nickel chemistries reduce or eliminate cobalt needs

faq.question: Why can't cobalt simply be sourced from other countries?
faq.answer: The Congo holds the largest reserves and lowest extraction costs. Other deposits exist in Australia and Canada but are more expensive to mine, making complete geographic diversification economically difficult.

faq.question: How are battery makers reducing their cobalt dependence?
faq.answer: Manufacturers are shifting to LFP chemistry which uses no cobalt, increasing nickel ratios in NMC cells to minimize cobalt content, and investing in recycling to reclaim cobalt from spent batteries.
